headline: Shifting manufacturing offshore to Mexico and Hungary, signalling a structural change in where Chinese-brand vehicles are produced even as volumes on global roads keep rising
reasoning: BYD is opening factories in Mexico and Hungary, reflecting Beijing's broader strategic shift to establish Chinese car manufacturing presence outside China rather than relying purely on exports. This means that even as BYD vehicle numbers on roads globally continue to grow, China's raw export statistics may understate BYD's actual market penetration. Australia, being geographically close to China, is still likely to receive a large proportion of its vehicles directly from Chinese factories.
quote: What has actually happened is that Beijing has started shifting its priorities and it's looking to produce fewer of these cars or to grow the share of cars produced in China slower and have more of a Chinese car manufacturing presence in other countries. So we're now starting to see BYD factories open in Mexico and Hungary. And so more and more of the the world's Chinese cars are actually being produced outside of China.
episode_title: Why Chinese EVs are taking the wheel down under

headline: Australia becoming a key destination for Chinese EVs as tariff-free market, with high petrol prices accelerating consumer shift toward EVs and hybrids
reasoning: Australia has seen a surge in Chinese vehicle imports partly because major markets like the US, Canada, EU, and Brazil have imposed steep tariffs on Chinese EVs, redirecting flows to tariff-free destinations like Australia. Additionally, high petrol prices are driving Australian consumers toward EVs and hybrids, where China is the dominant global supplier. Australia's lack of a domestic car manufacturing industry weakens the rationale for protective tariffs.
quote: One of the reasons we found so many Chinese vehicles come into Australia just in the last year is that more and more countries have started imposing these tariffs. And so China's been looking for new tariff free destinations that can be sending cars to. So for us to send them to the US and Canada, they got clamped down on, started sending them to the EU, they got clamped down on. Brazil was up, they got clamped down on in Brazil and now we're getting more in Australia and we don't have it as big a domestic car manufacturing industry to protect in Australia. So the rationale for tariffs is is a lot weaker here.
episode_title: Why Chinese EVs are taking the wheel down under

headline: Chinese EV export dominance set to soften as tariffs restrict destinations and Beijing pivots policy focus toward AI and higher-end technologies, though BYD volumes on Australian roads will keep growing
reasoning: Ben Udy notes that on the demand side, many markets are imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs, reducing the number of destinations China can freely export to. On the supply side, Beijing is signalling a strategic shift away from EV and vehicle manufacturing generally, redirecting focus toward higher-end technologies, particularly AI-related industries. This dual pressure means China's dominant export growth in vehicles is likely to soften over the coming years. However, he distinguishes between the macro export trend and the retail presence of specific brands like BYD, which he expects to continue growing strongly on Australian roads.
quote: On the demand side, a lot of markets are imposing tariffs and so there are fewer destinations that China can freely export to. And on the supply side, Beijing is sort of signalling that they're shifting their focus away from EVs and vehicle manufacturing generally and towards higher end technologies, in particular AI related technologies. And so for a long time Beijing has had a real strategic focus on dominating vehicle markets and that has supported the the surge in growth of vehicles out of China. Now we're starting to see that that sort of policy, policy push start to shift away and towards other markets. Instead, China is shifting manufacturing to other destinations. And so we're likely to see China's, China's export growth dominance sort of soften over the next few years. But don't expect to see fewer, fewer Byds on the road. That's that's going to keep growing pretty strongly for a while.

headline: Tariffs on Chinese EVs in the US, Canada and EU have been effective at suppressing direct imports but China finds workarounds — e.g. switching to hybrids/petrol cars not covered by EV-specific tariffs
reasoning: Where tariffs have been applied — US (~100%), Canada (~100%), EU (steep rates) — they have sharply reduced imports of targeted Chinese EVs. However, China has responded by exporting non-EV vehicles (hybrids, petrol) to the same markets where those are not covered, and by shifting manufacturing to third countries. The EU example shows that tariff effectiveness is limited when China can pivot product mix or production geography.
quote: If we look at the EU for example, what we saw after they imposed tariffs on Chinese made EVs is that China exported a lot fewer EVs to the EU but started exporting a lot more vibrants and and petrol cars that were not covered by the EV. headline: GDP growth expected around 0.2% for Q2, with a per capita recession possible given prior quarter contraction — below RBA's ~0.5% expectation
reasoning: Net trade is expected to contribute 0.1 percentage points to GDP, while government spending was positive but soft. The overall picture points to GDP growth of around 0.2%, well below the RBA's expectation of around 0.5%. On a per capita basis, a contraction is possible; combined with last quarter's per capita GDP contraction, Australia could technically be in a per capita recession. This is described as a 'technical blip' but not a positive signal.
quote: When we add everything all together, the picture's looking, uh, pretty weak. Um, I think we'll get GDP growth of around 0.2%. Maybe a bit more. But, um, it's definitely going to be on that low positive side. Um, we're not expecting a contraction in GDP, but once we take that into per capita terms, it wouldn't be surprising at all to see a contraction. And given that we saw a contraction in per capita GDP last quarter, that would mean that, uh, if we do get a contraction in per capita GDP this quarter, we'd be experiencing a per capita recession.
episode_title: Australia’s trade deficit gets a fuel injection

headline: Current account deficit widened to $27.2bn in June quarter, driven by surging oil import costs and record EV imports, partially offset by higher coal and LNG export prices
reasoning: Australia's current account deficit blew out primarily because oil prices surged, making import bills much larger. Record electric vehicle imports also added to the deficit. While the Middle East conflict boosted export prices for coal and LNG, that uplift was insufficient to offset the oil import surge. Australians also switched away from long-haul European travel to cheaper regional destinations, reducing outbound tourist spending by around 12%, though this did little to offset the overall trade imbalance.
quote: Australia's imports are more expensive, as is sort of the main headline. Um, mostly oil prices are way up. And so the amount that we are spending on, uh, imports of oil, it's, it's way up. Uh, that means Australia's imports ballooned and that means the deficit got larger. The the conflict in the Middle East did also boost the price of a lot of Australia's exports, including coal and LNG. But that impact was nowhere near big enough to offset the big rise in, uh, in oil imports.
episode_title: Australia’s trade deficit gets a fuel injection

headline: Outbound Australian tourist spending fell ~12% year-on-year — first dip since Covid — as high oil prices and Middle East conflict reduced long-haul flight availability to Europe
reasoning: The data showed a striking drop in Australian tourist spending abroad, down about 12% from the prior year, marking the first decline since Covid. The actual number of travellers was roughly unchanged, but Australians shifted from expensive long-haul European trips to cheaper, shorter regional destinations like Vietnam, Indonesia, and New Zealand. Fewer Middle East stopovers were available due to the conflict, reducing European route capacity. The net effect was a significant decline in total outbound spending, while the offsetting fall in inbound European visitors was not large enough to compensate.
quote: The number of Australians or the, amount of, uh, tourist money that was spent overseas by Australians was way down about 12% down from from last year. Um, and the first time that we've seen a dip in tourist numbers, uh, since since Covid... because fewer Australians were looking to go to Europe and the USA, get into that warm summer climate. And that's because of the high cost of travel. Um, as well as the lower, lower availability of routes.

Oxford Economics expects the September meeting to remain live but believes the RBA will more likely wait until November before acting. Stubborn inflation continues to be the overriding concern.
